After removing 30 percent of the nodes at random (here D and F, drawn dashed with their edges), the surviving graph has split into the triangle A, B, C and the pair E, G." width="100%"} Creates a new graph with a fraction of nodes removed uniformly at random, along with all of their incident edges. This is the basic operation of *site percolation* and models random failures: servers going down, people being immunized or leaving a social network, stations closing in a transport network. Comparing the surviving graph with the original (for example, with `largest_component_size()`) shows how well the network holds together when nodes fail at random. Typical uses include: - stress-testing the robustness of a network to random node failures - running many randomized trials to estimate how connectivity decays with `q=` - generating perturbed versions of a graph for sensitivity analyses The number of nodes removed is `round(q * n)`, where `n` is the node count, so the removed fraction is exact up to rounding. Every node is equally likely to be removed; for targeted attacks (removing hubs first), select and delete nodes by a centrality score instead. For a whole sweep over `q=` with averaging, see `percolation_threshold_analysis()`. The original graph is not modified. The returned graph keeps the directedness of the original, and surviving nodes and edges keep their IDs, labels, weights and attributes. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [q]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fraction of nodes to remove, between `0.0` and `1.0` inclusive. For example, `q=0.2` removes 20% of the nodes. `q=0.0` returns a copy of the graph structure and `q=1.0` returns an empty graph. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Seed for the random number generator. Calls with the same graph, `q=`, and `seed=` remove the same nodes, which makes results reproducible. If `None` (default), a fresh random seed is drawn on every call. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new Graph containing only the surviving nodes and the edges between them. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `q=` is outside the range `[0.0, 1.0]`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The graph below is two clusters (A, B, C and E, F, G) held together by the hub D. Removing 30% of its seven nodes takes out two of them; with this seed one of the casualties is the hub, so the survivors fall apart and the largest connected piece is just the triangle E, F, G: ::: {#2109fba4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("D", "F"), ("E", "F"), ("E", "G"), ("F", "G")]) ) percolated = graph.node_percolation(q=0.3, seed=9) survivors = sorted(percolated.get_node_df()["label"].to_list()) (survivors, percolated.largest_component_size()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (['A', 'B', 'E', 'F', 'G'], 3) ``` ::: ::: A single draw says little on its own. Repeating the removal over many seeds and averaging the size of the largest component gives a robustness estimate; as `q=` grows, the surviving graph keeps less and less of the original seven nodes in one piece: ::: {#bb9fe989 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def mean_largest_component(q, trials=200): sizes = [ graph.node_percolation(q=q, seed=s).largest_component_size() for s in range(trials) ] return sum(sizes) / trials {q: mean_largest_component(q) for q in [0.0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.45, 0.6]} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {0.0: 7.0, 0.15: 5.4, 0.3: 4.245, 0.45: 3.155, 0.6: 2.3} ``` ::: :::
